name: New Mexico

events.title: Statehood
events.text: New Mexico became the 47th state on January 6, 1912.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, New Mexico kept 1 seat in the House. It elected its one member statewide (at-large).

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, New Mexico's House delegation grew from 1 to 2 seats.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 78th through 90th Congresses (1943–1969), New Mexico elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, New Mexico kept 2 seats in the House.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, New Mexico kept 2 seats in the House.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, New Mexico kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, New Mexico's House delegation grew from 2 to 3 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, New Mexico kept 3 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, New Mexico kept 3 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: State court draws map after veto
events.text: The governor vetoed the legislature's congressional plan in October 2001, and no replacement passed. A state district court drew the districts in January 2002 in Jepsen v. Vigil-Giron.

events.title: Court-drawn map after legislative impasse
events.text: When the legislature did not enact a congressional plan after the 2010 census, a Santa Fe County district court issued the districts on December 29, 2011, in Egolf v. Duran.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, New Mexico kept 3 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Citizen committee proposes, legislature enacts
events.text: A 2021 law created a seven-member Citizen Redistricting Committee to recommend maps. The legislature, which could adopt or change its proposals, passed a congressional plan based on the committee's Concept H, signed December 17, 2021.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, New Mexico kept 3 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: State supreme court allows gerrymandering claims
events.text: In Grisham v. Van Soelen, the New Mexico Supreme Court held that partisan gerrymandering claims can be heard under the state constitution. On remand a trial court found the 2021 map did not dilute votes enough to fail the court's test, and the high court affirmed in November 2023.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c091.text: New Mexico's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1968 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which raised New Mexico's seats from 2 to 3. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which left New Mexico with 3 seats. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map following: State court draws map after veto. The governor vetoed the legislature's congressional plan in October 2001, and no replacement passed. A state district court drew the districts in January 2002 in Jepsen v. Vigil-Giron.

c113.text: New map following: Court-drawn map after legislative impasse. When the legislature did not enact a congressional plan after the 2010 census, a Santa Fe County district court issued the districts on December 29, 2011, in Egolf v. Duran.

c118.text: New map following: Citizen committee proposes, legislature enacts. A 2021 law created a seven-member Citizen Redistricting Committee to recommend maps. The legislature, which could adopt or change its proposals, passed a congressional plan based on the committee's Concept H, signed December 17, 2021.
